text: Why effects? Because a handler gets the rest of your program, called k.
What it does with k decides what the effect means.
The running example: a summary, then a picture.
The workflow yields Chat and Draw. It never says who answers them.
Handlers answer by resuming k. Each next example adds one handler around it.
Drop it: a cost cap of three cents, around every model call.
Chat costs one cent. The cap passes it on.
Draw would bring it to five. So the cap answers itself, and drops k.
The image model is never called.
Ask again: retry performs the effect once more, on the handlers outside it.
The provider times out twice. The third attempt answers.
Then k resumes once, with the answer that worked.
Keep the answers: effects are data, so a recorder can file each answer.
Replay runs from the tape, with no provider at all.
An effect it has never seen stops the run.
Hold it: the scheduler is a handler that keeps the k of each waiting task.
Tea sleeps every two hours, stretch every three. The clock parks each k.
When every task waits, the clock jumps to the next wake-up.
Six hours in under fifteen milliseconds, the same lines every run.
With dependency injection, an injected client answers a call, and returns.
It never gets the rest, so it cannot drop it, or hold it while others run.
Plain async spreads: whatever awaits must be async, and so must its callers.
With effects, total size yields Spawn and Gather. No async, no await.
A handler decides how Fetch is answered. Both give thirty-six.
Effects are rows, and handlers columns. Each handler minds one concern.
A new effect is one row. A new concern is one column.
With dependency injection, each check mark would be a wrapper class.
Effects are not free. For code that runs one way, plain Python is better.
When you need to steer the rest of the program, use a handler. pip install doeff.
